title: Does the largest digit always have to be the multiplier?
description: Three different digits are written as letters, the smallest first and the largest last. The six ways are grouped in pairs, two place value expansions show which way wins, and four, six and eight confirm it. Keeko doubts the plan of putting the biggest digit in the tens place.
teaching_notes: One idea: expand each number as tens plus ones and compare the matching parts, so the largest digit is the multiplier and the other two go in decreasing order for any three digits. Watch for students who put the biggest digit in the tens place of the two digit number.

source: Show that qp × r is the largest product for digits p < q < r
video_script.why: The child sees that algebra settles the question for every set of three digits, not only two, three and five.
video_script.substitution: Write the digits as p, q and r with p < q < r, group the six ways by multiplier, expand by place value and compare, then try 4, 6 and 8.
video_script.anchor: the frame of two boxes times one box, now filled with the letters p, q and r
video_script.wrong_answer: the biggest digit in the tens place
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko puts the largest digit in the tens place and leaves the middle digit to multiply, which gives eighty six times four.
video_script.payoff_line: The largest multiplication answer is queue pee times ar

final_answer.spoken: queue pee times ar is the largest, and for four, six and eight it is sixty four times eight, which is five hundred twelve

maths_rules: digits p < q < r; qp means 10 × q + p
six ways grouped by multiplier: qr × p and rq × p; pr × q and rp × q; pq × r and qp × r
larger tens digit gives the larger number: rq × p, rp × q, qp × r remain
rp × q = (10 × r × q) + (p × q); rq × p = (10 × r × p) + (q × p); p × q = q × p; r × q > r × p because q > p; so rp × q > rq × p
qp × r = (10 × q × r) + (p × r); rp × q = (10 × r × q) + (p × q); q × r = r × q; p × r > p × q because r > q; so qp × r is the largest
slip: biggest digit in the tens place gives 86 × 4 = 344, less than 512
video_script.design: One idea: for any three digits the largest is the multiplier and the others go in decreasing order. The letters p, q and r and the three finalists stay on the board. Keeko's doubt is to put the biggest digit in the tens place.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the frame of two boxes, a times sign and one box; three digit cards with question marks

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.frame: the frame of two boxes times one box appears
marks.ask: three blank digit cards appear beside the frame

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='frame'/>With two, three and five, the largest digit was the multiplier. The other two went in decreasing order.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Will this happen for any three different digits?

beats.on_screen: the frame and the blank cards stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the cards become p, q and r with p < q < r; qp means 10 × q + p; the six ways in three pairs: qr × p and rq × p; pr × q and rp × q; pq × r and qp × r

marks.letters: the three cards turn into the letters p, q and r in order of size
marks.tens: q p is written as ten times q plus p
marks.pairs: the six ways appear in three pairs by multiplier

beats.colours: each pair in its own colour
narration: <bookmark mark='letters'/>Call the digits pee, queue and ar, with pee the smallest and ar the largest.
<bookmark mark='tens'/>The number queue pee means ten times queue plus pee.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>The six ways make three pairs, one pair for each multiplier.

beats.on_screen: Given: digits p < q < r, each used once, in (two digit) × (one digit)

marks.given: the three digits and their order are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three digits with pee less than queue, and queue less than ar.

beats.on_screen: To show: which way gives the largest answer; then check with 4, 6 and 8

marks.find: the aim and the check are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the way that gives the largest answer. Then we check it with four, six and eight.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: keep the number with the larger tens digit in each pair: rq × p, rp × q, qp × r

marks.keep: the larger number of each pair stays and the others fade
marks.three: the three finalists are written in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='keep'/>Step one, keep the number with the larger tens digit in each pair. The same multiplier works on it.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Three ways are left, ar queue times pee, ar pee times queue, and queue pee times ar.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: rp × q = (10 × r × q) + (p × q); rq × p = (10 × r × p) + (q × p); q > p, so rp × q is larger

marks.expand: both ways are expanded by place value
marks.ones: p × q and q × p are boxed as equal
marks.tens: 10 × r × q is shown larger than 10 × r × p

narration: <bookmark mark='expand'/>Step two, split ar pee times queue and ar queue times pee by place value.
<bookmark mark='ones'/>Their last parts, pee times queue and queue times pee, are equal.
<bookmark mark='tens'/>The first parts are ten times ar times queue, and ten times ar times pee. Queue is bigger than pee, so ar pee times queue wins.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: qp × r = (10 × q × r) + (p × r); rp × q = (10 × r × q) + (p × q); r > q, so qp × r is larger

marks.expand: the two ways are expanded by place value
marks.same: the two first parts are boxed as equal
marks.rest: p × r is shown larger than p × q

narration: <bookmark mark='expand'/>Step three, compare queue pee times ar with ar pee times queue.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Their first parts, ten times queue times ar and ten times ar times queue, are equal.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Their last parts are pee times ar and pee times queue. Ar is bigger than queue, so queue pee times ar wins.
<bookmark mark='win'/>Step four, check with four, six and eight. Sixty four times eight is four hundred eighty plus thirty two.
<bookmark mark='mid'/>Eighty four times six is four hundred eighty plus twenty four, which is five hundred four.
<bookmark mark='low'/>Eighty six times four is three hundred twenty plus twenty four, which is three hundred forty four.

beats.on_screen: Answer: qp × r is always the largest; for 4, 6 and 8 it is 64 × 8 = 512

marks.ans: the answer qp × r is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The largest multiplication answer is queue pee times ar.
<bookmark mark='num'/>For four, six and eight, that is sixty four times eight, which is five hundred twelve.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the frame
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 86 × 4; 344 is written and set beside 512

marks.fix: the multiplier 8 glows as reaching both digits of 64

beats.colours: the wrong way in the warning colour
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the biggest digit in the tens place is best. That gives eighty six times four.
<bookmark mark='test'/>But that gives only three hundred forty four, far below five hundred twelve.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The multiplier works on both digits, so the biggest digit belongs there.
